Backups & restore

A backup is a copy of the panel's database: users, nodes, settings, the audit log and the secrets in it.

Treat a backup as secret material

The database holds node API keys and the Telegram bot token as written — there is no at-rest encryption, by design, because encrypting them would only move the key to another file on the same host. What protects them is the filesystem: the data and backup directories are 0700, and the database and every backup .db copy are 0600. Move any off-site copy over an encrypted channel.

Take a backup now

Backups land in /var/lib/ovmanager/backups, and the newest 14 are kept unless you change that. Reaching for the panel's web UI is not required at any point — which matters, because the usual moment you want a backup is the moment the panel is unhappy.

A backup is a plain .db file named ovmanager-<label>-<stamp>.db, written 0600: a consistent SQLite snapshot taken through the online-backup API — safe while the panel is writing — staged in a temporary file and only then published under its final name. The newest copies beyond the keep count are pruned as they are made. Restores stage and verify the candidate with PRAGMA quick_check and a schema check before it replaces anything, so a truncated or edited backup is refused rather than restored over your live data.

A daily backup

This is a systemd timer, so it keeps running even if the panel is stopped. The panel has its own scheduler too, under Settings → Backup — off by default, with its own time and retention. Using both is redundant; pick the one that matches how you operate, and remember that only the timer survives a stopped panel.

Off-site copies

A daily backup on the same disk is not a backup. The scheduled backup can push the newest backup to another machine: fill in a target like backup@server:/backups/panel and, after each backup (the daily timer, and any manual ovmanager backup), the newest file is copied there with rsync (or scp when rsync is not installed).

  • The transfer uses plain SSH with key-based login and BatchMode — no password prompts, ever.
  • The target machine must already accept your key, and the target folder must already exist.
  • Success or failure is written to the Audit Log. Nothing else on the remote side is created, rotated or cleaned up — retention is yours to manage there.

Restoring

From the CLI

ovmanager restore with no name lists what is available and changes nothing. Naming a backup restores it, with the service stopped and restarted around the swap.

From the panel

Settings → Backup accepts an uploaded backup and restores it atomically:

  • Writes are refused — HTTP 503 — until the swap has finished, so nothing is half-written against a database being replaced.
  • The database being replaced is kept as a fallback.
  • The restored database is migrated on the spot, so an older backup comes back at the current schema version rather than needing a manual step.

What is in a backup, and what is not

ItemBacked up by ovmanager backup
Users, expiry, quotas, tagsYes — in the database
Nodes and their API keysYes — in the database
Settings, admin accounts, audit logYes — in the database
Panel TLS key and certificateNo — they live outside the database
VPN users, certificates and configsNo — those live on each node, under /var/lib/ovnode and /etc/openvpn

So a complete disaster-recovery plan has two halves: the panel database here, and each node's own state. Back both up, and remember that node data is only rename-safe if you keep the same --name.
